entries.title: A terminal for everyone
entries.event_semantics: The Dartmouth Time-Sharing System became operational in 1964; the feature follows its educational deployment through the 1960s. This is not a claim to the invention of time-sharing or to the first educational game.
entries.summary: At Dartmouth, sharing the computer changed who could learn to use it.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: In November 1964, Dartmouth's alumni magazine described a frustrating routine: deliver punched cards, wait for a batch to run, return for the result, then repeat everything after discovering a mistake. John Kemeny, Thomas Kurtz and Dean Leonard Rieser wanted access that fitted teaching rather than the operator's queue. Their system paired a GE 235 with a Datanet 30 handling communications. A student could submit work from a terminal while other people used the same equipment. The expensive computer stayed shared; the exchange became personal.

The magazine explained this arrangement through an imagined economics professor and student asking different questions of the same banking data. Their requests could be interleaved, with answers returned to separate teleprinters. By November, twenty-two stations were operating across departments and professional schools, including one at Hanover High School. That distribution was part of the design. A person did not have to enter the machine room, meet its operator or specialise in computer engineering before trying a calculation and responding to what came back.

Dartmouth's institutional timeline records seven secondary schools joining an experimental educational network in 1964. Among them were Hanover High School, Mascoma Valley Regional and Phillips Exeter. The equipment linked classrooms to a computing resource they did not each have to purchase. In 1968, another student project brought a terminal to a swimming meet: Andrew Behrens and Anthony Dwyer wrote the scoring program, and Thomas Morton entered results beside the pool. Shared computing could answer a local, practical problem as well as a formal exercise.

The library's history also restores the students behind the service. Undergraduates maintained DTSS as systems programmers, learning by working on the infrastructure other students used. Kemeny and Kurtz promoted access comparable to an open library, but that access depended on this continuing labour. Even the famous first-run story needs care: the library notes that neither professor remembered attending the celebrated early-morning session in May 1964. The durable achievement was a working service, supported by people whose names easily disappear behind a machine's specifications.

entries.title: The classroom after hours
entries.event_semantics: 1973 marks Woolley's Notes release and Brown's Talkomatic prototype, within a longer PLATO educational programme. Later recollections and institutional histories are identified as such.
entries.summary: PLATO's users turned shared educational equipment into a social place.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: PLATO began as an educational project at the University of Illinois, but its community depended on decisions about physical equipment. Don Bitzer, Gene Slottow and graduate student Robert Willson developed a plasma display that helped move terminals beyond a single classroom. Connections reached other campus buildings, Parkland College and local schools. The university's history describes a mainframe expansion in 1972 that opened the way to many more simultaneous users. A lesson now took place on equipment that also connected its learner to other people.

In summer 1973, Paul Tenczar asked seventeen-year-old programmer David Woolley to replace an unruly bug-report file. Anyone could edit it, and someone could erase everybody else's comments. Woolley's replacement attached identities and dates to messages, then allowed conversations rather than a single official reply. Released that August, Notes made reporting a fault into a shared discussion. Its origins were practical: people needed to ask for help and preserve answers. Safeguarding authorship was part of making that conversation useful, not an optional social decoration.

That autumn, Doug Brown demonstrated Talkomatic, and Woolley helped develop its channels. Characters appeared while people typed; separate horizontal windows kept simultaneous participants legible. Five people could contribute to a channel while others watched. Active participants could protect a conversation and decide who else entered. These were consequential interface choices. A channel had speakers, an audience and a boundary, even though everyone used the same larger system. Woolley's account describes a place to linger and meet whoever arrived, alongside the institution's scheduled educational work.

The extra uses also created competition for a shared resource. Illinois's history records games being restricted during peak teaching hours, leaving nights and weekends for play. Students taking quizzes, writing software and meeting friends were all drawing on the same infrastructure. Giving learners and course authors access to tools encouraged experimentation; deciding when that experimentation could happen remained an institutional negotiation. PLATO's social life did not require its educational purpose to disappear. It required rules about how different groups would occupy the terminals together.

entries.title: A cave made of decisions
entries.event_semantics: 1976 is a year-level anchor for Crowther's 1975–1976 work; Woods's expanded version is dated to 1977 by recovered-source research. No precise original publication day is asserted.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: Will Crowther translated a place he knew into a program people could explore through short commands. Dennis Jerz's research compared recovered source files with the Kentucky cave, showing both correspondence and deliberate adjustment. Routes became easier to describe; physical geography became a sequence of choices the program could recognise. A player encountered the cave through prose rather than a continuous visual field. Reading a room and choosing a direction were therefore practical navigation skills. The description supplied the information from which the next action had to be made.

The surviving original unsettles a familiar division of labour. Crowther did not simply provide a scientific cave model to which Don Woods later added imagination. Jerz found magic, humour, combat and puzzles already present. Woods expanded that mixture. Recovered files and interviews place Crowther's work in the 1975–1976 academic year and Woods's expansion in 1977. Woods had recalled 1976 in 2001; Jerz records his later agreement with 1977. Version evidence changes how we tell the story of a program that changed hands and circulated.

In his 2001 interview, Woods recalled hearing about a copy on a Stanford Medical Center computer and bringing it to the artificial-intelligence laboratory's machine. Operating-system differences required repairs before he could play. The game named Crowther, so Woods tried electronic mail addresses at network hosts until he reached him and received the source. This account places maintenance and correspondence before creative expansion. The collaboration depended on identifying another person's work and asking about it, rather than treating an anonymous circulating program as material without an author.

Woods described puzzles as his particular strength and said he preferred games as a hobby. He also resisted a neat literary origin story: he had read Tolkien, but denied consciously modelling his volcano on Mount Doom. His recollection helps keep the game's influences from becoming a formula. Adventure combined its authors' interests without requiring every room to represent an outside text. He had never played Dungeons & Dragons before working on Adventure; people later introduced him to role-playing because they thought its author would enjoy it.

entries.title: Who shares the dark?
entries.event_semantics: Autumn 1978 is Bartle's retrospective date for Trubshaw's first MACRO-10 version. The feature follows revisions into 1980, a 1985 published account and a clearly labelled 2017 reflection.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: Roy Trubshaw's first MUD at Essex was a small collection of connected places where people could move and talk. In his 1990 history, Richard Bartle distinguishes it from the better-known BCPL rewrite completed around Easter 1980. An intervening version let people add rooms and commands during play, but unrestricted additions could undermine exploration and the world's coherence. Openness created a design problem, not an automatic community. The program needed a way to let several people inhabit it without every new command unmaking what others had come to explore.

A shared room also needed shared consequences. Bartle recalled an early anomaly: one person's torch did not let the other person see. Adding containers, inhabitants and scoring meant making the world's rules work across participants, rather than copying a solitary adventure for several users. Even elevated authority grew from a tool: the designers' debugging mode became the power available to experienced wizards. The same machinery that helped an author inspect a new area could later change a player's relationship to everyone else inside it.

Bartle's March 1985 magazine account describes what that authority allowed. A wizard could watch another player's screen without their knowledge through a feature originally intended to expose usability problems. The account treats the resulting spectatorship as entertainment and an incentive to progress. Reading it now raises a specific question about consent, rather than proving that all early players agreed on privacy. A world made from text still had unequal powers. Its designers were choosing who could observe others, who could interfere and how those privileges were earned.

In a 2017 Essex interview, Bartle described a further ambition: freedom from the social constraints he associated with working-class life in 1970s Britain. This is his later account of the project, not a recorded statement from every early player. He also recalled a division of interests, with Trubshaw drawn toward the world's underlying behaviour and himself toward its content. MUD's identity experiment was built through that collaboration. What a participant could become depended both on imaginative possibility and on the quite specific rules these people wrote.

entries.title: The work behind a cartridge
entries.event_semantics: August 1976 is the documented contract/program-printout month, rather than a precise cartridge launch day. The feature follows surviving records through 1982 without treating archive coverage as continuous employment.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: Joyce Weisbecker learned programming on FRED, the experimental computer built by her father, RCA engineer Joseph Weisbecker. After high school, she took paid contract work for RCA in 1976. This arrangement matters as much as the family connection. The programs were commissioned work, undertaken by someone whose contribution can be followed through her own records. The Strong's account identifies two Studio II projects, TV School House I and Speedway–Tag. Her work sat between a household where computing was familiar and a company preparing software for a consumer machine.

Those cartridges asked different things of their players. TV School House I was a two-person quiz that also needed a printed question booklet. Speedway–Tag combined racing and chasing, again for two participants. The computer did not have to contain every part of an activity to organise it. A booklet could supply questions while the machine handled the contest. The museum records payments of $250 for each project. These small, specific commissions make the programmer's labour visible without turning her into an unsupported universal claim about who worked first.

The surviving paperwork gives that labour a sequence. The Strong's finding aid lists an August 1976 quiz printout, an agreement with amendments, and tag/speedway printouts from October and November. A December purchase order identifies developing and coding the Studio II program as professional services. Each kind of document answers a different question: what was commissioned, what was delivered and what the company agreed to purchase. The cartridge alone cannot show those relationships. Beside it, these records restore decisions and obligations that its small plastic shell conceals.

The archive also complicates a short console-only career story. Its inventory lists later VIP software orders and invoices from 1978 and 1979, followed by 1982 correspondence about copyright claims for the Studio II games. The finding aid's summary describes contract programming in 1976–1977; the dated contents reach beyond that summary. Those are distinct pieces of evidence, not grounds to invent an unbroken job. They let the exhibition follow software after its initial delivery, through later commissions and the continuing administrative life of authorship.

entries.title: A name inside the box
entries.event_semantics: 1982 anchors the surviving Pitfall! manual that demonstrates the credit policy. The feature concerns the early Activision publishing model; it does not invent a precise company-founding day or repeat a complete corporate history.
entries.summary: Authorship helps players choose a game.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: David Crane remembered Activision's credit policy as a reason for creating a company, rather than decoration added after success. In his Good Deal Games interview, he credited president Jim Levy's record-industry experience with promoting the people behind the products. Crane preferred the comparison with a book publisher: a player who liked one author's work could look for another game by that person. The name supplied a way of choosing. This was a deliberate publishing strategy, not proof that no earlier game had ever acknowledged its maker.

Crane's account also resists the image of an author working untouched by colleagues. Designers had their own projects, but tried one another's games and argued over details. He recalled giving Pitfall! a single life shortly before release, until other people persuaded him to allow more attempts. The individual credit and the shared workshop therefore belong together. A recognisable style could emerge from one programmer's decisions while still being tested, criticised and improved by the people sitting nearby. Public authorship did not make collaboration disappear from production.

The Pitfall! instruction booklet brings that relationship into the player's hands. It names Crane as designer, lists earlier games and presents advice from him. The advice is specific: consider travelling left, learn the underground routes and plan a route. This is more useful than a signature attached to an unexplained product. A credited maker explains how to approach the challenge he constructed. The printed page lets a player connect a difficult route, a repeated attempt and an individual voice without needing to know how the cartridge's code works.

The same booklet offers entry to Pitfall Harry's Explorers' Club for reaching 20,000 points and sending a photograph of the television score. Its author-addressed advice ends by inviting players to write. The exchange required a camera, a letter and someone receiving the post; it was not an automatic online achievement. A score could become an object to share outside the living room. The club tied performance to the publisher's identity, while the named designer gave that relationship a human address inside an otherwise mass-produced box.

entries.title: The machine meets its location
entries.event_semantics: 1972 is the Pong field-test/early production anchor. Specific recollections come from 2008 and 2012 oral histories; no exact first-test day or unsupported coin-drop total is asserted.
entries.summary: A working game still had to survive players, operators and collection day.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: Ted Dabney's account includes work that rarely fits a game screenshot. He and Nolan Bushnell bought a route of pinball machines, pool tables and other amusements from a Nutting salesman. Collecting those machines' takings helped support them without their old salaries. A location was therefore already a working relationship, not an abstract market. Someone had to own the equipment, place it, collect the money and keep it usable. A new electronic game entered that routine of physical and commercial obligations.

Dabney recalled putting the early Pong prototype into a small cabinet and adapting a laundry-machine coin mechanism. Later machines could go into places on the route. His oral history moves backwards to distinguish that first installation from a subsequent batch of prototypes, a useful warning against treating every remembered number as a production ledger. Testing meant watching an object operate away from its workbench. The cabinet, payment interface and venue mattered alongside the ball on the screen. Failure could come from the container as readily as from the circuit.

Al Alcorn remembered another lesson in the paddle controls. An inexpensive potentiometer wore out after heavy use. Counting coins and estimating the many knob movements within each paid game revealed a much harsher duty cycle than a brief workshop demonstration suggested. The team sought a more durable component. This was feedback expressed through a damaged part rather than a written player survey. A successful attraction demanded more engineering because people kept touching it. The physical gesture that made the game accessible also became a recurring maintenance requirement.

Service habits could cause trouble too. Alcorn recalled early machines with external power supplies returning after operators adjusted the visible voltage control while trying to improve sound or picture. Integrating the supply into the board reduced that opportunity for damage. His explanation connects circuit design with the people expected to maintain a cabinet. The lesson was specific and expensive: supplying a functioning prototype did not guarantee a dependable product. What happened after installation could change the hardware that eventually left the workshop for the next location.

entries.title: Learning the new box
entries.event_semantics: 1977 anchors the Atari VCS manual edition; the paired Fairchild manufacturer booklet dates to 1976. This comparative feature is about household operation, not a universal first-cartridge claim.
entries.summary: Manuals teach a household to play.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: The Atari VCS owner's booklet begins before any game can start. Its diagrams address different television antenna connections, explain the TV/Game switch box and show where the controllers belong. The household television was existing equipment with its own fittings and habits. Buying a console did not replace that arrangement; it added another use that had to be connected and later switched away. The drawings turn installation into a sequence a household can follow. Their prominence shows how much instruction belonged outside the game program itself.

Once a cartridge was inserted with the power off, more choices remained. Atari's booklet explains a numbered Game Select display, separate difficulty switches for the two players and a reset switch that starts the chosen game. It sends the owner back to the individual game's instructions for what those settings mean. The console supplied a common vocabulary of controls, while each cartridge interpreted it. A box that could host different games therefore needed a continuing partnership between its physical switches, the screen and the paper placed beside it.

Fairchild's 1976 booklet calls the console programmable, but its opening examples make that word concrete. For the built-in Hockey game, numbered buttons answer on-screen prompts about the game, time limit and speed. An owner can accept defaults or select options before starting. This is programming as the booklet presents it to a player: configuring an activity through a controlled conversation with the machine. It does not mean that every buyer is writing software. The distinction helps recover what a flexible game system actually offered within an ordinary evening.

The Fairchild controller also changes meaning with the activity. In Hockey, the booklet maps movement, twisting and vertical knob action to players and goalie, with diagrams explaining how these motions can combine. Optional Videocart software extends the system beyond its built-in Hockey and Tennis. The hand stays around the same object while the instructions change what that object does. Comparing the two manufacturers' booklets makes interchangeability tangible: a continuing household device, new rules arriving with software, and people learning how to connect the two.
